BackDown indexes your drives, finds what's duplicated across all of them, and tells you, with a SHA-256 hash behind every claim, which drives are safe to wipe. Drives and scans, the time slider, hashes and proof, what "safe to wipe" means, recognised things and where they came from, the daemon, and drive health. The ideas the rest of the docs rely on. Each section says what BackDown does, and what it doesn't.

A root is a drive, or a top-level folder, that you've indexed: /media/old-drive , /mnt/nas , E:\ . BackDown calls it a drive and names it after the last part of its path ( old-drive ). Roots can't be nested inside each other: index each drive or top-level folder once. BackDown knows a root by its path. Plug a drive back in where it was mounted before and BackDown carries on with it; mounted somewhere else, it's a new root. A root whose folder is missing, or empty although it held files, counts as not connected: its files aren't read, and they wait for it. Indexing stays on one file system unless you pass --cross-filesystems , so a drive's scan doesn't wander into other drives mounted inside it. Symbolic links are neither followed nor recorded. backdown volumes next preview lists every disk and partition on the computer (model, serial number, file system, label, where it's mounted) and marks the ones the index covers. It only reads, and needs no administrator rights.

Every backdown index run records a scan of each root: every file's path, size and modification time, and on Linux and macOS its device and inode, so hardlinks are recognised. The files' contents aren't read while scanning. When you index a drive again: a file with the same path, size and modification time is unchanged, and keeps everything known about it, hashes included; a changed file gets a new version, and the old one is kept; a file that's gone is marked gone, and its last version is kept. A renamed or moved file counts as gone at the old path and new at the new one. A scan that's interrupted doesn't count; run the command again. Because every version is kept, the browser can show any folder as it was at any scan: that's the time slider at the bottom of a drive with two scans or more. An old version can be opened while its exact bytes still exist somewhere indexed, either the file itself, unchanged, or an identical copy (same SHA-256) on an indexed drive. Otherwise the index still remembers its size, dates and hash, but the bytes are gone. Hashing after each scan keeps that fingerprint; the daemon does it for you. If a drive that held files is suddenly empty, index refuses to record it: usually the drive isn't plugged in and you're looking at its empty mount point. If it really was emptied, pass --allow-empty .

Every claim BackDown makes about copies rests on SHA-256: two files are the same when their SHA-256 hashes are the same. Hashing everything would mean reading every byte on every drive, so hashing goes in three tiers: Size. A file whose size no other file shares can't have a duplicate, and is never read. Sample. For the rest, a quick fingerprint: the size, plus 64 KiB from the start, the middle and the end of the file. Files up to 192 KiB are read whole here, which gives their full hash straight away. Full SHA-256. Only files whose sizes and samples still match another file's are read completely. Hardlinks are one file: they're read once, and never count as each other's copy. Hashing runs one reader per file system ( --jobs 1 , right for spinning disks; raise it for SSDs). Files on drives that aren't connected wait for them. A file that can't be read is marked unreadable and skipped until backdown hash --retry-errors ; one that changed since it was indexed asks you to index again. dupes , check and the daemon run hash for you. The hash is SHA-256 throughout.

backdown check PATH says a drive (or a folder) is safe to wipe when every file in it has an identical copy outside it: another file with the same full SHA-256, outside PATH (a copy inside the drive you want to wipe doesn't count), and not just a hardlink to the same file. Files that couldn't be read block the verdict, because nobody knows what's in them. Empty files don't count against a drive. A file without a full hash counts as unique. check hashes everything that could have a copy first, so that only happens when no other file could be identical, or when its look-alikes are on drives that have never been connected while hashing. The verdict is about the index. A copy on a drive that isn't plugged in still counts, and a copy that went missing since its drive was last scanned would still count too. That's why freeing up a drive doesn't trust the verdict alone: before deleting a file, it reads the file and its copy again and compares them. check exits with 0 when the path is safe to wipe and 2 when files must be copied first, and lists the folders holding what exists only there ( --list names the largest 20,000 files).

BackDown recognises what things are, from the names and layout of files and folders: mail stores and Maildir mailboxes, Thunderbird profiles, Nextcloud data, Time Machine backups, iPhone and Android backups, operating systems, Mac, Linux and Windows home folders, websites, git repositories, database dumps, disk images, photo, music and video libraries, data exports (Google Takeout, Facebook, Instagram, Twitter, LinkedIn), downloads piles and recovered files. Each comes with its size, the years its files span and, where it's less than sure, how sure it is. Folders that programs can make again are flagged as regenerable : caches, thumbnails, node_modules , build output, virtual environments, trash and the like. They still count: a drive is only safe to wipe when they have copies too. A filing plan can leave them out, and then they stay on the old drive when you free it up. It also works out where things came from, and when, by reading small files on connected drives: Source What it says Backup scripts ( rsync , scp , rclone , cp -a , robocopy , tar ) Copied from which machine, with which tool, from which script iPhone backups' Info.plist Backed up from which device, which model, on which day Time Machine folder names Backed up from which computer, last on which day /etc/hostname , /etc/os-release Which machine a system disk was, which system git configuration A clone of which remote, on which branch GNU ddrescue map files Rescued from which device Database dump headers Dumped from which host, on which day Sync markers Kept in sync by Syncthing, Resilio Sync, Dropbox, Nextcloud or ownCloud Only small files are read (scripts up to 256 KiB, plists up to 8 MiB), and only on drives that are connected. backdown entities lists what's recognised; the daemon recognises each drive again after it's been scanned and hashed.

backdown overlaps shows how much of each drive, top-level folder and recognised thing already exists elsewhere, and where most of it is: "89% elsewhere: 89% on archive". It's the same SHA-256 test as check , summed up per place. The report and the filing plan use it to find what's already archived.

backdown daemon is BackDown running in the background. It: rescans each drive when it's due (every 24 hours by default; --rescan-every 12h , or never ), and as soon as a drive that was away comes back; hashes after every scan, then recognises what changed; serves the browser on 127.0.0.1 (port 8787), with a private link that backdown open opens; runs one job at a time, so the index has one writer and each drive one reader; rescues run beside the other jobs; with the next preview, reads every drive's health every six hours and tells you when one gets worse. It's killed safely at any point: jobs commit as they go and carry on where they stopped. backdown service install runs it for you, as you, with no extra rights: a systemd user service on Linux, and with the next preview a LaunchAgent on macOS and a task that starts when you log on on Windows. Until then, start backdown daemon yourself on macOS and Windows. On Linux, sudo backdown service install --system runs it for the whole machine instead (a NAS or a server): as a backdown user that can read every file and write none, sandboxed by systemd, with no network beyond this computer. Members of the backdown group can use it. The machine-wide service only reads: it never wipes and never rescues. While a daemon is running, it owns the index. index , hash , dupes , check , scans , status and apply --go are handed to it, and your terminal follows the progress. --local makes a command use the index directly. On Windows, terminal commands always use the index directly.

Drives say how they're doing, through SMART: sectors they've had to move or can't read, cable errors, wear on SSDs, temperature, and their own verdict. BackDown reads that for every physical drive without administrator rights, and without waking a drive that has spun down: through udisks2 on Linux (and smartctl where it's installed and allowed), diskutil on macOS, and the storage cmdlets on Windows. What it can't read, it says, with the command that would. Each reading is kept in the index under the drive's serial number, so a drive's history follows it from port to port and machine to machine, and what changed since the first reading shows as a trend: new bad sectors, rising cable errors, wear crossing 50, 80, 90 or 100%. A drive's verdict is ok , warning , failing or unknown . backdown health shows every drive, and exits with 2 when a connected drive is failing. The daemon reads them every six hours, when a drive appears, and when you ask ("Check now" in the browser). When a drive gets worse, a mirror stops matching its original, or a scheduled job fails, it's listed under Notifications in the browser's Activity view and, unless you untick "Show on the desktop", shown as a desktop notification: a few at most in any ten minutes and a dozen a day, except for a failing drive, which always gets through. A failing drive also gets a banner with Copy it now , which opens Rescue on that drive.

Delete only what has a verified copy elsewhere, move what exists only on the drive first, and see exactly what will happen before anything does. In the next preview backdown wipe and the browser's Free up view come with the next preview. In v0.2.0-alpha.4, backdown check tells you whether a drive is safe to wipe, and the deleting is up to you. Freeing up a drive is the one thing BackDown deletes, and only when you ask. The rule is simple: a file is deleted only when an identical copy exists outside what you're freeing, and both have just been read again and compared. What exists only on the drive can be moved somewhere first, or left where it is. It works on whole drives or on folders, so it also cleans up duplicates: free up the copy you don't want, and the one you keep is its proof.
1. Index everything that might hold copies

The copies have to be in the index. Index the drive you want to free and the drives that should hold its copies, then check it: backdown index /media/old-drive /media/archive backdown check /media/old-drive Copy check hashes what's needed and gives the verdict: SAFE TO WIPE , or COPY FIRST with the folders holding what exists nowhere else ( what "safe to wipe" means ). You don't need "safe to wipe" to go on, as long as you decide what happens to the rest.

Without --go , backdown wipe only shows what it would do: backdown wipe /media/old-drive Copy /media/old-drive 44 files, 182 MB 162 MB has an identical copy elsewhere: 99 MB in archive/Media, 60 MB in archive/Backups, 3 MB in archive/Documents 20 MB (7 files) exists only here: left in place (--move-to <folder> moves it first) Nothing was changed. To wipe: backdown wipe "/media/old-drive" --go --confirm "old-drive" Every file is re-read before it's deleted, and so is its copy (--trust-index skips that). Copy You can name several drives or folders at once. Copies inside what you've named don't count: they're going too.
3. Decide what happens to the files that exist only there

Either leave them, and they stay on the drive, or move them first with --move-to : backdown wipe /media/old-drive --move-to /media/archive/Unsorted Copy Each is copied to <move-to>/<drive name>/<its path on the drive> (here /media/archive/Unsorted/old-drive/Photos/2016/… ), read back to check the copy, and only then deleted from the old drive. The place to move to can't be inside what's being freed. For a tidier result, file the drive into your archive first; afterwards everything on it has a copy.

Add --go , and type the drive names the dry run showed after --confirm : backdown wipe /media/old-drive --move-to /media/archive/Unsorted --go --confirm "old-drive" Copy For every file, in turn: It must still be what the index says: same size and modification time. A file that changed, or is new since the last scan, is left alone. It's read again and hashed. If it no longer matches its hash, it's left alone. A copy outside the selection is found in the index and read again too. Only if it's there and identical is the file deleted. With no copy: with --move-to , it's moved (copied, verified, deleted); without, it's left. The deletion is written to BackDown's journal with its proof: which copy, its hash, and how it was checked. Folders the wipe leaves empty are removed; the drive's own top folder stays. Files that couldn't be read at the last scan are left in place. --trust-index skips the two reads: it checks that the copy is still there with the size and modification time it had when it was scanned, and trusts the hashes in the index. It's much faster and, right after a fresh scan and hash of both drives, nearly as safe, but a file that quietly went bad since its last hash wouldn't be noticed. Note A drive mounted read-only can't be wiped; the message says so. Remount it read-write first.

When the daemon runs the wipe, it rescans the drives involved afterwards. Without it, index the drive again. If the wipe removed everything, the drive is now empty, and indexing an empty drive needs --allow-empty : backdown index /media/old-drive --allow-empty Copy

backdown wipe stops before doing anything if what you named is: part of the running operating system: / , /usr , /etc , /var , /boot , /System , /Applications and the like, or anything else on the file system the computer runs from, outside the home folders; a whole home folder, such as /home/you or C:\Users\you (folders inside it are fine); on Windows, the system drive itself or Windows , Program Files or ProgramData on it; BackDown's own index, or the folder holding it; not on an indexed drive. Other drives are fine wherever they're mounted: /media , /mnt , /run/media , other drive letters. The machine-wide service never wipes; run backdown --local wipe … from your own account.

The Free up view does the same, with the daemon doing the work: Tick drives, folders, files or recognised things under "What to wipe". Each drive shows how much of it exists elsewhere; right-click anything in the browser and choose "Free up" to start from there. "What would happen" shows, for each, how much has an identical copy and where, how much exists only there, and anything that can't be wiped, and why. Under "What exists only here", choose "Move it first, to" a folder, or "Leave it where it is". The view shows the free space there. Under "Before deleting", "Trust the index" is the same as --trust-index . Type the drive names to confirm, and press Wipe . The wipe shows in Activity, and the view lists past wipes with what existed only there and what happened to it. The browser opened with backdown serve shows what would happen but can't wipe: that needs the daemon.
File your old drives into one archive

Let BackDown propose where everything on your old drives goes in one archive, and why, then copy it there with every file verified. Nothing is deleted. In the next preview backdown plan , backdown apply and the browser's Plan view come with the next preview. You have several old drives and want everything on them in one archive, sorted into something sensible, with nothing lost and nothing copied twice. BackDown does it in two steps: a plan that says where each thing goes and why, which you can read and change, then apply , which copies, reads every copy back to check it, and keeps a journal. Neither step deletes anything. Once the archive is indexed, the old drives can be freed up .
File your old drives into one archive

Index the old drives and the drive the archive will live on, so BackDown knows what's already there: backdown index /media/old-drive /media/laptop-2012 /media/archive backdown hash Copy The plan is built from what BackDown recognises : mail stores, phone backups, Time Machine sets, home folders, photo libraries and so on, with where they came from. plan recognises any drive that needs it, with the drives connected so it can read their backup scripts and plists; backdown entities shows you what it found beforehand, and the daemon keeps it up to date after every scan.
File your old drives into one archive

Name the archive folder, on the drive that will keep everything: backdown plan --to /media/archive/Archive Copy Plan 1: file 1 drive into /media/archive/Archive Copy 60 MB Disk image: VDI image (old-drive) /media/old-drive/VM/win10.vdi → /media/archive/Archive/DiskImages/old-drive/win10.vdi Disk image → DiskImages; newest file 2020 119 MB Folder (old-drive) /media/old-drive/Photos → /media/archive/Archive/Unsorted/old-drive/Photos not recognised as anything in particular: kept as it is, under its drive's name Drives old-drive 182 MB: copy 182 MB, already archived 0 B; every file will have a copy In all: 182 MB in 44 files. Next: `backdown apply 1` shows exactly what would happen; `backdown apply 1 --go` does it. Copy Every indexed drive except the archive's own is filed, unless you name some with --from (repeat it for several). Each item says what it is, where it goes, and why. The plan is saved; backdown plans lists the ones you've made. How things are placed Each kind of thing has a place in the archive, by type, then origin, then time. A mail store from mail.example.org goes to Mail/mail.example.org , an iPhone backup to Phones/<device>/<year> , a git repository to Code/<origin>/<name> . The origin comes from what BackDown found out about it (the server a backup script copied from, the phone's name, the computer's host name, a repository's remote); without one, it's the drive's name. Folders that aren't recognised as anything in particular keep their shape under Unsorted/<drive>/ , and loose files at a drive's top level go to Unsorted/<drive>/(top level) . A few rules keep the archive free of repeats: Already archived. Something whose bytes are already at least 99.9% inside the archive folder isn't copied: "already in the archive at …". Near twins. When two things of the same kind and origin are at least 90% identical (the same mailbox on two old drives, say), only what's unique to the second one is copied, into Also from <drive>/<name> inside the first one's folder. If it's all in the first, it isn't copied at all. Low-value piles. Downloads folders and recovered-file dumps ( found.000 , recup_dir , lost+found ) are listed, not copied. Caches (caches, thumbnails, build output, trash) are copied by default, because a drive can only be proven safe to wipe when every file has a copy. The browser's "Leave out caches, previews and build output" box, or skip_junk = true in a schema, leaves them out; they then stay behind when you free up the drive. Your own schema The places are a small TOML file you can change: backdown plan --print-schema > schema.toml backdown plan --to /media/archive/Archive --schema schema.toml Copy [place] mail-store = "Mail/{origin}" ios-backup = "Phones/{origin}/{year}" photos = "Media/Photos/{name} ({drive})" unsorted = "Unsorted/{drive}/{name}" # … one line for every kind [options] # downloads piles and recovered fragments: list them, but don't copy skip_low_value = true # regenerable caches, previews, build output and trash: copy them too skip_junk = false # a thing at least this identical to another of its kind and origin copies only its own files merge_overlap = 0.9 Copy Places are relative paths inside the archive, and can use {origin} , {name} , {title} , {drive} , {year} and {years} . Characters that don't belong in file names become - .

backdown apply 1 Copy Dry run of plan 1: 44 files (182 MB) to copy into /media/archive/Archive. Nothing was written. Run `backdown apply 1 --go` to copy. Copy The dry run reads the drives and writes nothing. It needs every source drive connected, says what's already done from an earlier run, what's already in the archive, and which destinations already exist, and checks the archive's drive has room.

backdown apply 1 --go Copy Each file is copied under a temporary name beside its destination ( .<name>.backdown-partial ), hashed as it's written, flushed to disk, given the original's modification time, renamed into place, then read back and compared. A copy that reads back differently is removed and reported. Along the way: an existing file at the destination is never overwritten: if it's identical it counts as already there, and if it differs it's left alone and reported as a conflict; nothing is ever deleted from the old drives; symbolic links aren't copied (the summary counts them); every file is written to a journal, so an interrupted run carries on where it stopped when you run the same command again. It ends with a summary, and exits with 2 when there were conflicts or failures to look at. When the daemon is running, --go is handed to it (you follow the progress in the terminal), and it indexes the archive afterwards.

Keep a folder, usually part of your archive, copied on another drive, with changed files' old copies kept aside and a sample re-read now and then. In the next preview backdown mirror comes with the next preview. An archive on one drive is one failure away from gone. A mirror keeps a second copy of a folder on another drive and checks it: new and changed files are copied and verified, nothing on the mirror is ever deleted, and a different sample of the mirror is read back regularly to catch copies that went bad.

backdown mirror add /media/archive/Archive/Mail /media/backup/Mail Copy Mirror 1: /media/archive/Archive/Mail → /media/backup/Mail Copy it now with `backdown mirror sync 1`; the BackDown service syncs daily and re-reads a sample every 30 days. Copy The first folder must exist; the mirror folder is created on the first sync. Neither may be inside the other. --verify-every 7 re-reads a sample every 7 days instead of 30.

backdown mirror sync Copy mirror 1: 1 copied (3 MB), 1 updated (old copies kept in .backdown-versions), 30 unchanged, 1 only on the mirror (kept) Copy Without a number, every mirror is synced. A file with the same size and modification time on both sides is unchanged. New files are copied and read back to check them. When a file changed, the mirror's old copy is first moved to .backdown-versions/<time>/ inside the mirror folder, so an accidental change on the original never destroys the only good copy. A sync never deletes. Files that exist only on the mirror (because they were deleted from the original, say) are kept and counted. Symbolic links aren't copied. Check the mirror drive has room: sync doesn't check free space first.

backdown mirror verify backdown mirror verify 1 --all Copy mirror 1: re-read 31 files (99 MB): all identical Copy By default a 5% sample is read back ( --percent 10 for more), and it's a different 5% each day, so repeated checks cover the whole mirror over time. --all reads every file. Each is compared with the original's hash in the index when that's current, or with the original itself. Missing files, different sizes or contents, and unreadable files are listed, and the command exits with 2.

With the daemon running, you don't need to run these by hand. Whenever both drives are connected, it syncs each mirror once a day and re-reads a 5% sample when a verify is due. The browser's Activity view lists the mirrors, whether both drives are there, and when each was last synced and verified. A verify that finds differences becomes a notification, and when a mirror's drive reports that it's failing ( drive health ), Activity says so and suggests a second mirror on a healthy drive. backdown mirror list Copy 1 /media/archive/Archive/Mail → /media/backup/Mail synced 2026-09-28 23:30 UTC: 31 files: 1 copied (3 MB), 1 updated (old copies kept), 30 unchanged, 1 only on the mirror verified 2026-09-28 23:30 UTC: re-read 31 files (99 MB, 100%): all identical Copy To stop keeping a mirror, backdown mirror remove 1 . The copies stay where they are.

Copy a failing drive or memory card safely, find deleted photos and documents by their contents, and look for lost partitions. BackDown only reads the drive. In the next preview backdown rescue and the browser's Rescue view come with the next preview. Three things can go wrong with a drive or a memory card, and Rescue has an answer for each: What happened What to do Command It's failing: clicks, freezes, read errors, very slow Copy it into an image first, the good areas before the bad backdown rescue image Files were deleted, or it was formatted Find photos, videos and documents by what's inside them backdown rescue find It looks empty, or a partition vanished Look for file systems the partition table no longer lists backdown rescue partitions Rescue only ever reads the drive. Whatever it saves goes to another drive: it refuses to write the image or the files it finds onto the drive being rescued. Careful If a drive is failing, every read counts. Copy it into an image first, then look for files and partitions in the image, not on the drive. BackDown can tell you a drive is failing before it stops: backdown health and the browser show what each drive reports about itself ( drive health ), and a failing drive gets a banner with Copy it now , which opens Rescue set up to copy it.

In the browser, the Rescue view lists every disk and partition. In a terminal, backdown volumes does, with model, size, serial number and file systems; or use lsblk on Linux and diskutil list on macOS. Drives are device files such as /dev/sdc on Linux or /dev/disk4 on macOS. Every rescue command also takes an image file instead of a drive.
When BackDown can't read the drive

Reading a whole drive directly needs a permission your account usually doesn't have. BackDown says so, and gives the one command that lets your account read that one drive, and never change it, until it's unplugged or the computer restarts: backdown: can't read /dev/sdc: reading a whole drive directly needs permission your user account doesn't have Run it as an administrator (sudo backdown rescue image …), or let your account read that drive: sudo setfacl -m u:you:r /dev/sdc Copy On macOS the command is sudo chmod o+r /dev/disk4 . On Windows, run the terminal as administrator. Running Rescue itself with sudo is fine too: it never opens BackDown's index, and what it writes is handed back to you rather than left owned by root.
Copy a failing drive into an image

backdown rescue image /dev/sdc /media/archive/Rescue/sdc.img Copy Copying /dev/sdc (500.1 GB) into /media/archive/Rescue/sdc.img The map: /media/archive/Rescue/sdc.img.map Ctrl+C stops it; run the same command again to carry on. Copy It works the way GNU ddrescue does. The first passes copy what reads easily, forwards and then backwards, skipping ahead past slow or bad areas instead of hammering at them. Later passes go back to the edges of the bad areas, then read what's left sector by sector, and finally retry unreadable sectors ( --retries 3 for more tries). Unreadable parts stay as zeros in the image. A map beside the image records what's been read, in GNU ddrescue's own format. It's saved every few seconds, so you can stop the copy at any time, or lose power, and run the same command to carry on where it left off. When it's done: Copied 500.1 GB of 500.1 GB; 12 KB couldn't be read, in 3 places. Running it again with --retries 3 tries those again. Copy It exits with 0 when everything was read, and 2 when some of it couldn't be. It won't start if: the image would be on the drive being rescued, or on another partition of the same physical drive ( --same-drive allows that for a drive that isn't failing); the destination doesn't have room for what's left to copy, or is formatted FAT32, which can't hold a file of 4 GB or more (it says so); an image of that name exists without its map (it's never overwritten).

backdown rescue find /media/archive/Rescue/sdc.img --to /media/archive/Rescue/sdc-files Copy This looks through every byte for the signatures of files, whatever the file system says: after files were deleted, the card was formatted, or the file system is damaged. What it recognises: Kind Types Photos JPEG, HEIC, PNG, GIF, WebP, BMP, AVIF, TIFF, camera RAW (CR2, CR3, NEF, ARW, DNG, ORF, RW2, PEF, SRW, RAF) Videos MP4, MOV, M4V, 3GP, AVI, MKV, WebM, WMV, MTS, TS, MPEG, OGV Audio MP3, M4A, WAV, FLAC, Ogg, Opus, AIFF, WMA Documents PDF, Word, Excel and PowerPoint (old and new), OpenDocument, EPUB, Outlook messages Archives ZIP, RAR, 7z Other SQLite databases, other Office-format files --only photos,documents narrows it to groups or types ( --only jpg,pdf ). What's found is saved in a folder per kind, named after where it was found on the drive, with the list in found.jsonl : Found 1.3 K files (6.1 GB): 1.2 K photos, 40 videos, 12 documents In /media/archive/Rescue/sdc-files (the list: /media/archive/Rescue/sdc-files/found.jsonl) Copy Files found this way have no names, folders or dates of their own (photos and videos keep the dates inside them). A file that was stored in scattered pieces comes back damaged, or not at all: finding by content can't put pieces back together. A file whose end isn't found is kept up to a size limit for its type and counted as cut off. When the daemon does the finding, it indexes what it found, so the files open in the browser.

backdown rescue partitions /dev/sdc Copy It reads the partition table (MBR, including logical partitions, or GPT, checking both of its copies), then looks for file systems where partitions usually start, and at every sector with --deep (as slow as copying the drive). File systems are found by their own structures, including their backups when the start is damaged: NTFS, exFAT, FAT, ext2/3/4, XFS, btrfs, APFS, HFS+, F2FS, SquashFS, ReFS, ISO 9660 and UDF; encrypted LUKS and BitLocker volumes, LVM, RAID members and swap are recognised as such. /dev/sdc (500.1 GB): no partition table Starts at byte Sector Size File system Name In the table 1048576 2048 500.1 GB NTFS Photos NO: lost 1 not in the table. To get files out of one: backdown rescue find /dev/sdc --to <folder> --start <byte> --end <byte> Copy It never changes the partition table. To get files out of a lost partition, run rescue find on just that range (its start, and its start plus its size), or use "Find files in it" in the browser.

The Rescue view asks three questions: Which drive or card? Every disk and partition, or an image file. It checks BackDown can read it and, if it can't, shows the permission command with a Copy button and "Check again". What happened? "It's failing", "Files were deleted, or it was formatted", or "It looks empty, or a partition vanished". Where should it go? A folder on another drive (it suggests BackDown Rescue/<drive> <date> on one of your indexed drives), and what to look for. Rescues run in the daemon beside scans and hashing, show their progress (a copy shows a map of what's been read), can be stopped and resumed, and stay on the list afterwards. From a finished copy you can go straight to "Find files in the copy" or "Look for partitions in the copy". Rescues need the daemon; the machine-wide service doesn't do them, so run backdown rescue from your own account.

Rescue doesn't reassemble fragmented files or open a lost partition's file system directly. A copy that's an image file on an indexed drive can be opened in the browser, where the files on its FAT, exFAT, ext and NTFS partitions can be browsed ( disk images ).

The file browser shows everything in the index the way a file manager would, with history: every drive, every folder as it was at any scan, and a viewer for most files, without copying anything back first. It only reads. The browser listens on this computer only, answers only that link (the token becomes a cookie for the session), and makes no requests beyond this computer: the viewers are built in. With the daemon running, backdown open opens its browser instead, whose link stays the same across restarts. backdown serve --port 8788 runs a second one next to the daemon's.

Your indexed drives are in the sidebar, with their size and number of files. Folders open with a double click or Enter ; Alt+↑ goes to the parent, Alt+← back. Grid ( Ctrl+1 ) and list ( Ctrl+2 ) views show the folder; the details pane ( Ctrl+I ) shows a file's versions, its copies on other drives, and a preview. With the next preview there's more: a photo gallery ( Ctrl+3 ) and a size map ( Ctrl+4 ), filters by type, size and date, sorting, hidden files ( Ctrl+H ), tabs, typing a location ( Ctrl+L , where a drive's name stands for its path), right-click menus, and a dot beside each drive for its health . Press ? for every shortcut. From the right-click menu next preview , "Open with system app" opens a file in the program your computer uses for it, and "Show in file manager" shows where it is. The bar at the bottom of a drive with two scans or more is the time slider : drag it to see the drive as it was at that scan. Files deleted since are struck through, and those that changed later are marked. Back to now returns. A file's old version opens if its bytes still exist: the file itself, unchanged, or an identical copy on any indexed drive ("Read from … (identical copy)"). Otherwise the index still knows its size, dates and hash, and says the bytes are gone. The details pane lists every version of a file, with Diff against the current one for text. Compare… next preview shows what changed in a folder between any two scans: what was added, removed and changed, with a diff for text files. Files count as the same when their SHA-256 hashes match (or, before they're hashed, their size and modification time).

Ctrl+F searches the folder you're in and everything below it; Ctrl+Shift+F searches every indexed drive. It matches file and folder names, not their contents, ignoring case and accents; with several words, a name must contain all of them. Exact names come first, then names that start with what you typed, then the rest, newest first. Disk images open read-only, without mounting anything: raw images ( .img , .dd , .raw , .bin ), ISO discs, VHD, VHDX, VMDK, VDI, qcow and Apple disk images ( .dmg ). Browsing never writes to your drives. Everything that changes something (copying into an archive, freeing up a drive, rescuing, rescanning) happens in the daemon and is described in its own guide. The browser opened with backdown serve can't do those; it says which command to run instead.

Where BackDown keeps its index, how often the daemon rescans, notifications, running it for the whole machine, and adding a Pro licence key. BackDown has no settings file: the few things you can change are options on the commands, and the daemon's are set where it's started. There's no settings screen in the browser either; it remembers your view, sort order, details pane and hidden-files choice in your web browser.

The index is one SQLite database, index.db , in your BackDown data folder: System Data folder Linux ~/.local/share/backdown (or $XDG_DATA_HOME/backdown ) macOS ~/Library/Application Support/BackDown Windows %LOCALAPPDATA%\BackDown Linux, machine-wide service /var/lib/backdown The folder is readable only by you: the index lists every file path on your drives. backdown status shows which index is in use. To use another one, pass --db to any command, or set BACKDOWN_DB : backdown --db /media/archive/backdown/index.db status export BACKDOWN_DB=/media/archive/backdown/index.db Copy Previews before 0.2.0-alpha.3 kept backdown.db in the current folder. BackDown mentions it if it finds one; keep using it with --db backdown.db , or index again.

The daemon rescans each drive every 24 hours, and as soon as a drive that was away comes back. --rescan-every changes the interval ( 30m , 12h , 7d ), and never rescans only when a drive comes back or you ask. --port moves the browser from port 8787. The service installed by backdown service install starts backdown daemon without options. On Linux, to change them, override its command with a systemd drop-in: systemctl --user edit backdown Copy [Service] ExecStart= ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/backdown daemon --rescan-every 12h Copy Then systemctl --user restart backdown . backdown service install --print shows the unit it installs. To keep the user service running while you're logged out: loginctl enable-linger $USER Copy On macOS and Windows next preview , the service runs while you're logged in: a LaunchAgent ( ~/Library/LaunchAgents , with its log in ~/Library/Logs/BackDown ) or a scheduled task named "BackDown" that starts it, without a window, when you log on. It uses the daemon's defaults; for other options, run backdown daemon --rescan-every 12h yourself instead.

The daemon keeps a list of what's worth knowing: a drive whose health got worse, a mirror that no longer matches its original, a scheduled job that failed. It's under Notifications in the browser's Activity view, with read and unread. "Show on the desktop" there turns desktop notifications on or off; the list is kept either way. The choice is saved in notifications.json in your data folder. The machine-wide service doesn't pop anything up: it isn't on anyone's desktop.

On a NAS or a server, one daemon can index the whole machine for everyone: sudo mv backdown /usr/local/bin/ sudo backdown service install --system sudo usermod -aG backdown alice Copy It runs as a backdown user that can read every file and write none, with the whole file system read-only to it except its own folder, /var/lib/backdown , and no network beyond this computer, all enforced by systemd. Members of the backdown group can use it with the usual commands and backdown open (after logging in again). It doesn't wipe or rescue: do those from your own account with --local . backdown service status (with --system for this one) says whether it's installed and running and what it's doing; backdown service uninstall removes it and keeps the index.

The legacy index is the `index` folder the pre-Rust scripts wrote: <vol>/chunks.list bd-plan.py's crawl plan, one `R<TAB>dir` or `F<TAB>dir` per line; its first line, `F<TAB>/mount/point`, names the drive's root <vol>/chunks/<id>.tsv one chunk, from `find -printf '%s\t%T@\t%p\n'`: size, mtime (seconds.fraction) and the raw path; <id>.done marks it finished <vol>.tsv every finished chunk, merged (read when present and up to date) hashes.db bd-hash.py's table h(path, size, mtime, sha256) Each volume becomes a root with one finished scan, dated from its chunks. Folders that belonged to another user on an old computer's disk are often closed to your account. Either: run the machine-wide service on Linux, which can read every file (and write none); or make the drive readable to you (on an old disk you own, sudo chown -R on the folders is common), then index again. Running sudo backdown index isn't a good fix: it would build a separate index in root's own data folder. Files that fail while hashing are marked unreadable and skipped from then on. backdown hash --retry-errors tries them again, for example after reconnecting a flaky drive. A file that changed since the last scan asks you to index again. On macOS, some folders (Mail, Photos, Messages and others in your Library) are protected by the system. Give your terminal Full Disk Access in System Settings > Privacy & Security, or they show up as unreadable.

Rescue reads the drive itself ( /dev/sdc ), not its files, which needs more than an ordinary account has. BackDown says so and gives the command that lets your account read just that drive until it's unplugged: sudo setfacl -m u:$USER:r /dev/sdc on Linux, sudo chmod o+r /dev/disk4 on macOS. sudo backdown rescue … works too. See Rescue .

The browser's sidebar lists drives you've indexed. Some things to check: It isn't mounted. Does BackDown send anything anywhere? No. It needs no account, sends no telemetry, and makes no network requests. The browser listens on 127.0.0.1 only. Principles has the rest. Does it change my drives? Indexing, hashing, checking, browsing and recognising only read. BackDown writes when you ask it to: copies into your archive ( apply ), to a mirror ( mirror sync ), and what Rescue saves, always to the destination you chose. It deletes only when you free up a drive, and only files with a verified copy. Can it index a NAS or a network share? Yes, anything mounted as a folder. Indexing reads names and sizes over the network, and hashing reads the contents of files that could be duplicates, so it's slower than a local disk. Index the mount point itself. Does it make backups? It copies and verifies: into one archive, and to mirrors. Scheduled, encrypted, versioned backups to other disks or the cloud are planned , not built yet. Does it work on Windows and macOS? The command-line preview does: indexing, hashing, duplicates, check , the browser and the daemon. The five rules BackDown is built on, and how the program keeps them. Five rules don't change from one version to the next. This page says what each one means in practice, in the program you can download.
1. Never write to a source drive

The drives BackDown looks at are only read. Indexing reads names, sizes and dates; hashing, recognising, checking and browsing read contents; none of them write. The browser only reads too: everything that changes something goes through the daemon, and happens only when you ask. When BackDown does write, it's to a place you named, never to what it's reading from: copying into an archive writes into the archive folder, and never overwrites a file that's already there; a mirror sync writes to the mirror, and moves a changed file's old copy aside rather than replacing it; Rescue writes the image and the files it finds to another drive, and refuses to write onto the drive being rescued. On Linux, the machine-wide service makes this a rule the system enforces: it runs with the whole file system read-only to it, except its own folder. The one exception is the one you ask for: freeing up a drive deletes files from it, under rule 2.
2. Never delete without a verified copy

BackDown deletes in one place, freeing up a drive , and only a file that: is still what the index says it is; has an identical copy outside what you're freeing, and both have just been read again and compared (or, if you choose, the copy is still there exactly as last scanned); or has just been moved, with the copy read back and checked first. Every deletion is written to a journal with its proof: which copy, its SHA-256, and how it was checked. It refuses the running system, whole home folders and its own index, shows what would happen before anything does, and asks you to type the drive names.
3. Every long job can resume, and shows why it's slow

Drives drop off USB buses and computers restart. Scans and hashing save as they go, copying keeps a journal, and a drive image keeps a map of what's been read, so running the same command again carries on where it stopped, and the daemon can be stopped at any time. The terminal and the browser's Activity view show what's running, how far it is, what's waiting, and which files wait for a drive that isn't connected.
4. The free edition answers "what do I have, and what's duplicated?"

Knowing what's on your drives and what's duplicated is the free part of BackDown, and it's complete: every drive indexed, duplicates found across all of them, a SHA-256 behind every "this has a copy". The command-line preview is free. Pricing shows what's planned for the paid tiers.

BackDown runs on your computer and needs no account. It sends no telemetry and makes no network requests: the only connections it makes are to itself, on 127.0.0.1. The browser listens on 127.0.0.1 only, answers only its private link, and loads nothing from elsewhere. A Pro licence key is checked on your computer, by its signature. On Linux, the machine-wide service is cut off from the network beyond this computer by the system. This is about the program. The website, backdown.io, is covered by its privacy policy .
